pages.heading: Gauss–Seidel iterative method — idea and diagonal dominance

blocks.text: Start with initial guesses for the unknowns in a system \(AX=B\). For three unknowns:
Gauss–Seidel gives successive approximations to the solution. A standard sufficient condition for rapid convergence is strict diagonal dominance.

A system is strictly diagonally dominant if, in each equation, the absolute value of the coefficient chosen on the diagonal is greater than the sum of the absolute values of the other coefficients in that equation:
Check whether the equations are arranged so that the diagonal coefficient in each row dominates the remaining coefficients. If necessary and possible, reorder the equations before iterating.
Step 2 — Solve each equation for its diagonal unknown
Take the initial approximation \([x_1^{(0)},x_2^{(0)},x_3^{(0)}]=[0,0,0]\), unless another starting vector is specified.
Step 3 — Use each new value immediately
Step 4 — Repeat until the required accuracy is reached
Continue Step 3 until two successive approximations agree to the specified number of decimal places.

blocks.label: PankusDesk tip
blocks.title: When do I stop iterating?
paragraphs: There is no fixed number of Gauss–Seidel iterations. Compare each new approximation with the previous one and continue until all unknowns have stabilised to the required accuracy.
If the question specifies an accuracy, use that. If it asks for 2 decimal places, stop when two successive approximations give the same values to 2 d.p.; similarly for 4 d.p. or any stated tolerance.
If no accuracy is stated, use 3 decimal places as the working convention for these problems. Stop only when every unknown agrees to 3 d.p. in two successive iterations.
bullets: Do not decide the number of iterations in advance.
Check all unknowns, not just one of them.
A system may settle in 3 iterations, or may need 5, 6 or more.
blocks.example: For example, \((2.0002,1.0001,-0.9999)\) and \((2.0000,1.0000,-1.0000)\) are identical to 3 decimal places, so the iteration can stop.
